paragraphs: Hello, I'm Seth For Privacy, and welcome to Season 2, Episode 12 of Opt Out. Opt Out's a show where I sit down with passionate people to learn why privacy matters to them, the tools and techniques they've found and leveraged, and where we encourage and inspire others towards personal privacy and data sovereignty. Have you been looking for a privacy-preserving and lightweight search tool that you can self-host? This episode, we're sitting down with Ben Bespey to chat about his project, Whoogle Search.

Welcome on to Opt Out, Ben. Thanks for having me, Seth. Yeah, I am very excited to chat about this because Whoogle is a tool that I've been using personally and that I've been hosting for kind of the community that's formed around this podcast and around the education work that I do on Twitter. So it's been one of my most used tools. I mean, it's my default search in all of my browsers, my WISE browser. It's definitely a heavy, heavy use tool for me.

So I'm really excited to learn more myself, but really just to get the word out there, get other people familiar with what Whoogle does, with what the approaches you've taken to building it are. And yeah, very excited to dive into that. But for those who aren't familiar with you, do you mind just introducing yourself and telling us a little bit about what Whoogle is? Sure. So I'm Ben Busby. I'm a freelance programmer, musician, and game developer that frequently works on open source projects, one of which is Whoogle, obviously.

It's just a, I mean, to boil it down, it's just a Google search proxy or meta search engine that grabs Google search results and filters out pretty much everything that you don't need, including like ads, tracking, JavaScript, AMP links, refer header, pretty much everything that like isn't really crucial to the search experience that I was annoyed by. And yeah, that's about it. Yeah. I think that's honestly one of the strengths of Whoogle is it's a very simple tool.

It's Google search without all the crap that you don't want to have to deal with. So it also makes it a very easy tool to transition people onto because if you're familiar with Google search, you can figure your way around Whoogle quite quickly. So before we dive too deeply into the tool itself, I'm really curious to learn a little bit more about you and kind of what kicked off Whoogle and just kind of what it was that woke you up to the need for personal privacy initially.

Sure. I guess as far as personal privacy and my interest in that goes, it kind of was born out of a frustration with the byproducts of lack of privacy. So the kind of things that were popping up, like, so I guess I should back up. Growing up, I wasn't interested in tech at all. I was like a musician and I kind of begrudgingly decided to major in computer science and just sort of going from this like hard break mindset of like, from just kind of treating the internet as like, oh, it's just my curiosity playground to like, oh my God, it's frighteningly easy to collect data on people and people are doing it and making just ridiculous amounts of money doing it.

That hard transition just really threw me in the deep end. And I was, I don't know, I just ended up feeling kind of violated. And I was like, I don't know, like search engines in general, I think everyone kind of treats them as a natural extension of their curiosity. And so to kind of violate that trust in someone and start using what they're curious about to sort of market to them better, I just find the whole thing gross. And I think most people do on some level, but I was fortunate in that I found it gross and also was able to do something about it.

And that sort of led to the creation of Google. I guess I can just sort of pivot right into that. And I mean, I guess on one level, Google was sort of born out of a frustration with mobile browsing. So I was like most people using Google search. And anytime I wanted to like share a link with someone, it was always an AMP link. And as someone who always inspects every link that I send or view or anything like that, I was having to manually edit these links all the time.

And so the very, very first iteration of Google, all it did was serve identical Google search results, but without the AMP link, like you just, it was doing the editing for me essentially. And then there were just, there was a very obvious snowball effect from that, where I was just like, oh my God, like I can just take everything I don't like about Google search and remove it and make a more lightweight, more immediate experience. Because I'm also someone who's extremely impatient.

If I want, if I search something, I want the very first thing I see to be what I'm looking for. And that just, there's just a reflex with normal Google search for you instinctively scroll past ads to get to what you're actually looking for. So yeah, I mean, it was a combination of impatience, hatred of AMP links, hatred of ads, just like, I don't know, I guess in general, I kind of gravitate more towards low tech things in general. Like if it were up to me, the entire browsing ecosystem would be closer to like Gemini or something where it's more plain text based anyways.

So it was just kind of my contribution where I could get rid of annoyances myself. And as a byproduct, have a product that I can share with other people and allow them to do the same. Yeah. And that's one of the beautiful things about the free and open source space. And obviously, Google is open source. It's just that you can kind of take your personal need, build something out of that. Obviously, you have the talent to build that and you've done great work there.

But you can build that product and allow other people to benefit from the things that came out of your own frustration, which I feel like is the source of so many of the tools that we end up using out of the free and open source space. If someone gets fed up with the centralized or the closed source alternative, builds a tool that fits their specific needs, their specific wants. And that ends up being a tool that's so helpful to other people. And I'm glad you touched on the search angle and how the invasion of privacy there, it really hits on even further details than just the facts about who you are.

Like, it's not just your name. It's not just your address. It's not those things which are important that you have the choice who gets access to those. But like you mentioned, it also even hits on your curiosities and even the things that are pre-belief. They're pre-part of your identity. There's a lot there that even before you know something about yourself, a search engine where you're putting all of these queries, where you're putting all these searches, can learn that about you and be able to leverage that against you for their own monetary gain, which is really a disgusting concept but has become the crux of a lot of the internet today.

Yeah. I mean, it's just gross. I don't know how anyone can kind of sleep at night and contribute to that sort of thing. But here we are. It's definitely an unfortunate thing that the internet turned out like that. But obviously pivoting back to Whoogle, I'm thankful that there are ways that we can start taking steps for ourselves.
